ap_microeconomics-m01.stem: Why are cartel agreements among oligopolists often unstable?

options.text: A cartel earns less than a competitive industry, so members leave it at once.
options.why: A cartel that holds together earns monopoly-like profit, more than competitive firms.

options.text: The demand for the cartel's product is perfectly elastic, so quotas have no effect.
options.why: Cartel demand is downward sloping; quotas raise the price.

options.text: The government requires every cartel to price at marginal cost, which ends the agreement.
options.why: Cartels are generally illegal, but they are not required to price at marginal cost.

options.text: Each member gains by producing extra output while the others keep their quotas.
options.why: Each cartel member has an incentive to cheat: producing more raises its own profit while the rest restrict output, which makes the cartel unstable.

options.text: Each member earns the same profit whether or not it cheats, so cheating does not matter.
options.why: Cheating raises the cheater's profit in the short run.

ap_microeconomics-m03.stem: Consider the following situation: The price of an input used to make notebooks falls, and sellers supply more notebooks at every price. Which of the following correctly describes the change in the market?

options.text: A movement along the supply curve, which is an increase in the quantity supplied.
options.why: Treats a change in an input price as a movement along the supply curve, which only a change in the good's own price causes.

options.text: A rightward shift of the demand curve, which is an increase in demand.
options.why: Attributes a change in production costs to the demand curve.

options.text: A leftward shift of the supply curve, which is a decrease in supply.
options.why: Reverses the direction of the supply shift when an input becomes cheaper.

options.text: A rightward shift of the supply curve, which is an increase in supply.
options.why: The price of an input is a determinant of supply, so a fall in it shifts the supply curve to the right.

options.text: A movement along the demand curve, which is an increase in the quantity demanded.
options.why: Confuses a cost-driven change in supply with a movement along the demand curve.

ap_microeconomics-m04.stem: A firm with market power sells the same product in two separate markets and can prevent resale. In Market A the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand is 2.0, and in Market B it is 4.0. Marginal cost is the same in both markets. To maximize profit, which statement is correct?

options.text: Market B should be charged the higher price, because its demand is more elastic.
options.why: Reverses the rule: the more elastic market should get the lower price.

options.text: Market A should be charged the higher price, because its demand is less elastic.
options.why: The profit-maximizing markup is larger where demand is less elastic, because buyers are less sensitive to the price.

options.text: The two markets should be charged the same price because marginal cost is the same.
options.why: With different elasticities, equal prices do not maximize profit.

options.text: Market B should be charged the lower price, because it has the larger total revenue.
options.why: Uses total revenue rather than elasticity to set prices.

options.text: Market A should be charged the lower price, because its buyers are less sensitive to price.
options.why: Reverses the implication of inelastic demand.

ap_microeconomics-m05.stem: The consumption of beekeeping near orchards provides benefits to people other than the buyers and sellers. Which of the following is true?

options.text: The market produces more than the socially optimal quantity of beekeeping near orchards, and a tax could move the market toward the efficient quantity.
options.why: Describes a negative externality.

options.text: The market produces the socially optimal quantity of beekeeping near orchards, because private benefits equal social benefits.
options.why: Private and social benefits differ when there is a positive externality.

options.text: The market produces less than the socially optimal quantity of beekeeping near orchards, and a price ceiling would correct the problem.
options.why: A price ceiling would reduce quantity and does not capture the external benefit.

options.text: The market produces less than the socially optimal quantity of beekeeping near orchards, and a subsidy could move the market toward the efficient quantity.
options.why: With a positive externality, marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so the market underproduces and a subsidy raises output toward the efficient level.

options.text: The market produces less than the socially optimal quantity of beekeeping near orchards, and a tax would increase efficiency.
options.why: A tax would reduce output further when the market already underproduces.

ap_microeconomics-m06.stem: A perfectly competitive firm faces the following condition: The market price is above average total cost at the profit-maximizing output. Which of the following is the best decision for the firm?

options.text: Shut down in the short run, because price is above the minimum of average variable cost.
options.why: A price above average variable cost is a reason to keep producing, not to shut down.

options.text: Continue producing and earn a positive economic profit, because price exceeds average total cost.
options.why: Price above average total cost means total revenue exceeds total cost.

options.text: Continue producing and earn zero economic profit, because competitive firms always earn zero profit.
options.why: Competitive firms earn zero economic profit only in the long run, after entry.

options.text: Produce zero output until price falls to average total cost.
options.why: A firm earning a profit at the current price should produce at the profit-maximizing output.

options.text: Continue producing at a loss, because price equals marginal cost.
options.why: Price above average total cost means the firm earns a profit, not a loss.

facts: cond=The market price is above average total

ap_microeconomics-m06.stem: A perfectly competitive firm faces the following condition: The market price is above average variable cost but below average total cost at the profit-maximizing output. Which of the following is the best decision for the firm?

options.text: Shut down in the short run, because the firm is earning an economic loss.
options.why: A loss alone is not the shutdown rule; the firm shuts down only if price is below average variable cost.

options.text: Continue producing in the short run, because price covers average variable cost and part of fixed cost.
options.why: Revenue covers all variable costs and part of fixed cost, so producing loses less than shutting down.

options.text: Continue producing and earn a positive economic profit, because price exceeds average variable cost.
options.why: Profit requires price above average total cost, which is not true here.

options.text: Shut down in the short run, because price is below average total cost.
options.why: Price below average total cost is a loss, but the shutdown rule compares price with average variable cost.

options.text: Expand output until price equals average total cost.
options.why: A competitive firm produces where price equals marginal cost, not where price equals average total cost.

options.text: Oligopoly
options.why: Mistakes interdependent behavior among a few firms for a market with many sellers or one seller.

ap_microeconomics-m08.stem: The graph shows two straight-line demand curves for two goods that cross at point A. The curves are labeled D1 and D2. Which of the following is true at point A?

stimulus.description: Two straight-line demand curves, D1 and D2, that cross at point A.

options.text: At point A, demand D2 is perfectly inelastic, because its slope is steeper.
options.why: A straight steeper line is still not vertical, so it is not perfectly inelastic.

options.text: At point A, the elasticity of demand D2 is larger, because slope and elasticity are the same thing.
options.why: Confuses the slope with the elasticity; elasticity also depends on the price-quantity ratio.

options.text: At point A, demand D1 is unit elastic, because the demand curve is a straight line.
options.why: A straight line has a different elasticity at each point and is not unit elastic everywhere.

options.text: At point A, demand D1 is more elastic than demand D2, because the same price change causes a larger percentage change in quantity along the flatter curve.
options.why: Elasticity = (1/slope) x (P/Q); at the same point the flatter curve has the smaller slope in absolute value and therefore the larger elasticity.

options.text: At point A, demand D1 and demand D2 have the same elasticity, because they cross at the same price and quantity.
options.why: Believes crossing at the same point implies equal elasticity; elasticity also depends on the slope.

ap_microeconomics-m11.stem: Which of the following statements about economic choices is correct?

options.text: A wealthy society can produce unlimited quantities of every good and does not face trade-offs.
options.why: Believes wealth removes scarcity; even rich societies have limited resources and face trade-offs.

options.text: A good that is free to consumers has no opportunity cost to society.
options.why: Treats a zero price as a zero cost; resources used to make the good have alternative uses.

options.text: Scarcity affects only the production of goods and not the use of time.
options.why: Limits scarcity to goods; time is also a limited resource that must be allocated.

options.text: On its production possibilities curve, producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.
options.why: With scarce resources, using more of them for one good leaves fewer for others, so a trade-off exists.

options.text: Opportunity costs exist only when money is paid for a good.
options.why: Ties opportunity cost to monetary payments; time and resources have opportunity costs without any payment.

ap_microeconomics-m11.stem: A student chooses to attend a concert tonight instead of studying or working a shift. Which statement best describes the opportunity cost of attending the concert?

options.text: Zero, because the student values the concert more than the alternatives.
options.why: Mistakes the benefit of the chosen option for a lack of cost; choices always have a forgone alternative.

options.text: The cost the concert organizers pay to produce the show.
options.why: Confuses the buyer's opportunity cost with the seller's production cost.

options.text: The total value of every alternative the student could have chosen.
options.why: Adds all alternatives instead of using only the next-best one.

options.text: The value of the best alternative the student gives up.
options.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone, here the more valuable of studying and working.

options.text: The ticket price and nothing else.
options.why: Counts only the explicit money cost and ignores the value of the time that is given up.

ap_microeconomics-m12.stem: The graph shows a firm's short-run cost curves. The curves are labeled MC, ATC, and AVC. Which of the following is true at point C?

stimulus.description: Short-run cost curves for a firm: marginal cost MC, average total cost ATC, and average variable cost AVC. Points A, B, and C are marked on the MC curve.

options.text: Marginal cost is below average total cost, so average total cost is falling.
options.why: Reverses the relationship between marginal cost and the average.

options.text: Marginal cost is above average total cost, so average total cost is rising.
options.why: At point C marginal cost is above ATC, which pulls the average up.

options.text: Marginal cost equals average total cost, so average total cost is at its minimum.
options.why: Marginal cost equals ATC only at the minimum of ATC, which is point B.

options.text: Average fixed cost is rising, because output is high.
options.why: Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises.

options.text: Average variable cost is above average total cost, because variable cost is part of total cost.
options.why: AVC is always below ATC; the gap is average fixed cost.

ap_microeconomics-m13.stem: The graph shows a firm's marginal cost (MC) and average total cost (ATC) curves. At which quantity is average total cost at its minimum?

stimulus.description: Short-run cost curves for a firm: marginal cost MC and average total cost ATC.

options.text: 0 units
options.why: Chooses the quantity where marginal cost is lowest, which is at zero output.

options.text: 20 units
options.why: MC crosses ATC at the minimum of ATC, at 20 units.

options.text: 10 units
options.why: Chooses a quantity where marginal cost is below average total cost, so the average is still falling.

options.text: 30 units
options.why: Chooses a quantity beyond the crossing, where marginal cost is above average total cost and the average has begun to rise.

options.text: 40 units
options.why: Chooses a quantity where marginal cost is above average total cost, so the average is already rising.
